prompt.context: Your firm has won an RFP to help a domestic airline carrier examine their in-flight connectivity (IFC) strategy. With 80% of US-based aircraft already outfitted with IFC technology and competitive pressures rising, offering WiFi service is becoming table-stakes. Your client has yet to enter the game, but they know it's something they need to consider to stay competitive.
prompt.question: What are some of the key things the client should think about when assessing their go-to-market strategy for IFC?

clarifying_info.q: What routes does the airline fly?
clarifying_info.a: The airline flies primarily domestic routes within the continental US, as well as select flights to Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
IFC includes only WiFi connectivity. In-flight entertainment (IFE) is delivered via an on-board server through a separate system, but the two can be integrated into one user experience.

clarifying_info.q: What is the airline's main objective?
clarifying_info.a: The airline's main objective is to stay competitive.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the airline's fleet and how many flights does it operate?
clarifying_info.a: The airline has 90 planes and services approximately 30,000 flights per year.

clarifying_info.q: How is IFC typically installed and managed?
clarifying_info.a: IFC is typically installed and managed by an outside vendor, either through a branded service (e.g., gogoAir) or a wholesale, white-label solution (e.g., Row44). Contracts are typically 10+ years long.

clarifying_info.q: Do different vendors use different technologies?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, different vendors use different technologies, which vary in quality.

clarifying_info.q: How does bandwidth work when multiple passengers are connected?
clarifying_info.a: Total bandwidth is shared across passengers, so the more passengers buy a session, the slower the service. Some carriers intentionally charge high prices to limit usage and ensure better service.

clarifying_info.q: What does one WiFi session cover?
clarifying_info.a: One session buys a passenger WiFi connectivity for the duration of the flight.

framework: Pricing and pricing model (free, ad-supported, pay per data usage, pay per time, pay by speed tier, subscription service)
Market demand — take rate and market segments
Costs — upfront capital investment and ongoing operating costs
Vendor contract structure — revenue/business model, split of investment costs and Opex, branding, contract length, technology
Product/user experience — built-in screens vs. BYO-screen, white-label vs. vendor-branding, speeds available, interoperability with in-flight entertainment, add-on services like calling or texting
Technology — speed, bandwidth, latency, availability when flying over water
Go-to-market — rollout timing, marketing, crew training, ad sales

questions.prompt: Question 1: Your analyst has pulled benchmarks on what two competitors are doing today (Exhibit 1). What are your thoughts on these two models?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare and contrast the two models using pros/cons. Strong candidates recognize these are not the only possible models and consider elements beyond those listed in the exhibit (e.g., cost structure, technology, product features, interoperability with IFE). Competitor 1 model pros: less operational burden on airline, potential for customer experience continuity (e.g., allow subscriptions across airline carriers), limited costs. Competitor 1 cons: limited control over pricing (high price could drive low take rates and anger customers), brand fit considerations. Competitor 2 model pros: control over pricing, control over user experience, potential for better ROI, easier to integrate with airline's other products (e.g., in-flight entertainment system). Competitor 2 cons: more operational burden on airline, higher costs. Other considerations: who will pay for the initial investment, what is the ongoing cost structure, potential to adopt more than one model across the fleet, technology limitations (vendors don't come equal).

questions.prompt: Question 2: The client has decided to partner with a white-label IFC vendor to outfit all 90 planes. The airline and vendor will share the initial investment, and the airline will pay the vendor a per-session fee to cover operating expenses. What percentage of passengers need to purchase a session for the airline to break even in 2 years?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for missing data (capex per plane, airline cost share, margin per session) before calculating. Advanced candidates will proactively question the 100% seat occupancy assumption and the assumption that all aircraft are outfitted simultaneously. Candidate should react to the resulting take rate and offer strategic implications given that industry take rates are only 5-10%.

math.setup: Break-even equation: Total passengers in 2 years x take rate x margin per session = Total investment. Data given only if asked: Capex = $250K per plane (airline covers 40%); Margin = $10 per session. Assumptions: seat occupancy = 100%, all aircraft outfitted at same time, ad revenues baked into margin figures.
steps: Airline share of investment per plane = $250K x 40% = $100K
Wide-body passengers in 2 yrs = 300 seats x 2,500 flights/yr x 2 yrs = 1,500,000
Narrow-body passengers in 2 yrs = 100 seats x 27,500 flights/yr x 2 yrs = 5,500,000
math.answer: 12.9% take rate required to break even in 2 years

questions.prompt: Question 3: Market research shows take rates are only between 5% and 10% today for paid connectivity. What do you think are the key drivers of IFC take rate?
questions.guidance: This is a correlation question — what variables might be correlated with higher take rates? Candidate should brainstorm across multiple categories and hypothesize the direction each variable would need to swing to drive higher take rate. Flight characteristics: flight length (longer = higher), flight time (red-eye vs. daytime), availability of other entertainment systems. Product characteristics: price (lower = higher take rate), speeds available, quality of service, number of connected devices allowed. Passenger characteristics: age, gender, income, cabin class (business vs. economy), business vs. leisure traveler.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key drivers of IFC take rate?

categories.name: Flight characteristics
ideas: Flight length — longer flights drive higher take rates
Flight time — daytime flights more likely to drive usage than red-eyes
Availability of other in-flight entertainment systems

categories.name: Product characteristics
ideas: Price — lower price drives higher take rate
Speeds available — faster speeds drive higher willingness to pay
Quality of service — reliable connectivity drives repeat usage
Number of connected devices allowed per session

categories.name: Passenger characteristics
ideas: Age — younger passengers more likely to use WiFi
Income — higher income drives higher willingness to pay
Cabin class — business class passengers have higher take rates
Trip purpose — business travelers have higher take rates than leisure travelers

recommendation: The airline should partner with a wholesale, white-label vendor to retain control over pricing and the user experience
Roll-out across aircraft should be gradual, with a potential pilot program to optimize pricing, user experience, etc.
Roll-out should prioritize newer planes that cover routes with high expected take rates
risks: Due to large upfront investment, the contract is likely to be 10+ years long, so smart vendor selection is very critical
Difficult to strike a balance between maximizing revenue and maintaining a sufficiently low take rate to ensure higher speeds
Technology is still nascent, with potential for poor user experience
